claims.text: CoFeNiV is a magnetic high-entropy alloy system.
An intermediate vanadium concentration optimizes the valence electron concentration in CoFeNiV.
Optimizing the valence electron concentration enhances diffusion barriers.
The intermediate-V optimum minimizes atomic mobility and suppresses high-temperature phase rearrangement and elemental segregation.
Both lower and higher V concentrations are less stable than the intermediate concentration.
The starting CoFeNiV nanoalloy is a homogeneous, single-phase material with a well-mixed elemental distribution.
Changing constituent levels in magnetic CoFeNiV can produce structural transitions associated with valence electron concentration.
Electronic-structure-driven diffusion barriers and local bonding environments control atomic mobility and phase stability.
The generalized Rigid Band Model can predict the majority phase in magnetic high-entropy alloys, including CoFeNiV.
Changing V content adjusts the valence electron concentration.
Changing the valence electron concentration modulates diffusion activation barriers.
An optimal electron concentration maximizes diffusion barriers, thereby reducing high-temperature rearrangement and preserving chemical homogeneity and structural integrity.
Intermediate-V samples will retain a single-phase solid solution better than lower- and higher-V samples after heating.
Intermediate-V samples will show sharper XRD peaks than lower- and higher-V samples.
Intermediate-V samples will exhibit less elemental segregation than lower- and higher-V samples.
High-temperature stability will vary non-monotonically with V content and have a clear maximum within an intermediate V-content window.
The prediction is restricted to CoFeNiV heated at 600–900 °C in vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
Oxidizing atmospheres or substantially different temperatures may introduce additional mechanisms.
XRD, TEM with elemental mapping, and tracer diffusion measurements can be used to compare phase integrity, segregation, and diffusion barriers across V contents.
Failure of the intermediate-V sample to outperform both lower- and higher-V samples, or absence of a non-monotonic stability trend, falsifies the hypothesis.
